name: Albin Countergambit
summary: The Albin Countergambit (1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5) sacrifices a pawn to plant a cramping d4-pawn and generate sharp piece play.
intro: The Albin Countergambit arises after 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4, when Black gives up a pawn to establish an advanced, cramping pawn on d4 deep in White's position. In return for the material Black gains a lead in development, open lines and a host of tactical ideas, including the notorious ...Bb4+ and ...d3 tricks that have trapped many an unwary opponent. It is an aggressive, uncompromising answer to the Queen's Gambit favoured by players seeking to seize the initiative from the outset.
line: d4 d5 c4 e5 dxe5 d4

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The heart of the Albin is the wedge on d4. This advanced pawn cramps White's position, denies the natural c3 and e3 development squares to the knights and bishop, and serves as a long-term thorn that Black's pieces rally around. Black typically follows with ...Nc6, ...Be6 or ...Bg4, and ...Qd7, developing quickly and keeping the option of ...O-O-O to throw the whole army into the attack. The extra pawn on e5 is not easy for White to hold, and Black often regains it or obtains full compensation through activity.

Tactics permeate the opening from the very first moves. The most celebrated is the Lasker Trap, which can arise after 4.e3, when 4...Bb4+ 5.Bd2 dxe3 turns the tables; if White grabs with 6.Bxb4 then 6...exf2+ 7.Ke2 fxg1=N+ underpromotes to a knight with a winning attack. More generally Black looks to advance ...d3 at the right moment, jamming White's coordination, while exploiting the half-open files and swift development. White must know the theory to sidestep these traps, aiming instead to blunt the initiative, return the pawn when useful, and reach a position where the extra material or a healthier structure can tell.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line runs 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3, when White fianchettoes the king's bishop to pressure the queenside, undermine the d4-pawn and develop safely; this restrained, positional treatment is considered White's most reliable route to an edge. Black continues with ...Be6, ...Qd7 and often ...O-O-O, massing forces for a central or kingside assault. A key idea is the manoeuvre ...Nge7-g6 to hit the e5-pawn and lend extra support to the advanced d-pawn.

Sharper attempts see White try to hold the extra pawn or challenge the centre directly, but these frequently invite the tactical resources for which the Albin is known. The thematic ...Bg4 pins the f3-knight to renew pressure on the centre, and the recurring break ...d3 can fracture White's coordination just as White hopes to consolidate. Throughout, Black's compensation is measured in initiative and activity rather than material, so accurate, energetic play from both sides is essential.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The countergambit is named after Adolf Albin, who employed 2...e5 in a notable game against Emanuel Lasker at New York in 1893. It was analysed and popularised in the following decades, with the Lasker Trap — named for Lasker and featuring an early knight underpromotion — becoming one of the best-known motifs in opening literature. Never a mainstream choice at the highest level, the Albin has nonetheless enjoyed periodic revivals, including outings by strong grandmasters seeking a fighting, theory-light weapon, and it remains a respected surprise try that can punish careless handling of the Queen's Gambit.

keyIdeas: 2...e5 counterattacks immediately, offering a pawn to seize the initiative.
After 3.dxe5 d4 Black plants a cramping, advanced pawn deep in White's camp.
The d4-wedge denies White the natural c3 and e3 development squares.
The Lasker Trap punishes a careless 4.e3 with a knight underpromotion.
Rapid development, ...O-O-O and the ...d3 break fuel Black's attack.
Compensation is measured in activity and initiative rather than material.

white: Develop calmly with Nf3 and g3, fianchettoing to pressure the d4-pawn.
Avoid the early e3 traps and refuse to grab material greedily.
Return the extra pawn when it defuses Black's initiative.
Blockade or win the advanced d4-pawn to leave Black without compensation.
Consolidate and let a healthier structure decide the endgame.
black: Support and rally pieces around the cramping d4-pawn.
Develop swiftly with ...Nc6, ...Be6 or ...Bg4 and ...Qd7, eyeing ...O-O-O.
Advance ...d3 at the right moment to jam White's coordination.
Exploit half-open files and tactical motifs against a slow White setup.
Play for the initiative rather than trying to regain the pawn at once.
